boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's engagement at Mariazell (8 November 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: the defeat of FML Count Merveldt's Austrian corps by the advanced guard of Marshal Davout's corps, from the surprise of Merveldt's column near Neuhaus to the rout below Mariazell and the pursuit toward Wegscheid. Merveldt's march from Steyer and Davout's march into the mountains are context, as are the retreat of Merveldt's remains to Graz and Fürstenfeld and the list of the Grande Armée at 6 brumaire. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) about 15,000 men under Marshal Davoust (Davout) and side B (Austrian) 7,000 men under GM Count Meerveldt (Merveldt). By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several, and the passages read do not show his basis. For side A, Davout's report and Schönhals have only the advanced guard under General Heudelet engage, and no passage read gives its strength (claim side-a-engaged); the passages read do not show whether Bodart's about 15,000 counts the whole of Davout's corps or the troops engaged. For side B, Davout's report gives Merveldt's corps as 6 battalions of grenadiers and 3 regiments of infantry (claim davout-side-b) and Schönhals gives 13 battalions and 6 squadrons leaving Steyer on 6 November, with no count of men (claim schoenhals-side-b); no passage read gives 7,000. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'victory of the French (about 15,000 men) under Marshal Davoust over the Austrians (7,000 men) under GM Count Meerveldt'.

claims.value: Side B (Austrian), the Austrian account's figures: Schönhals has Merveldt's corps camp at Steyer with 13 battalions and the 6 uhlan squadrons, while 6 battalions (2 Gyulai, 2 Peterwardein, 2 of the first Wallachian) and 6 hussar squadrons stayed at Gross-Ramming and Colonel Mariassy, with 6 battalions and 6 squadrons, took post at Steyer to defend the pass to Altenmarkt. 13 battalions and 6 squadrons left Steyer in two bodies late in the evening of the 6th for St. Georgen am Reith. At Lunz a battalion of grenadiers was posted on the road to Ipsitz and another on the road toward Gaming to cover the retreat. Merveldt reached Neuhaus at midnight with the head of the corps, the regiment Josef Colloredo and some grenadiers, only some hundreds of men; the greater part of the corps, overcome by fatigue, had broken up and stayed lying along the road. Schönhals calls the column caught in the defile below Mariazell six admittedly decimated battalions; that evening only two grenadier battalions, 200 men together, could be formed as a rearguard before Wegscheid. After the retreat the corps, including Khevenhüller's brigade, rose again to about 4000 men.
claims.rationale: Side B's own side's account (Schönhals writes after Austrian sources), read from the page images except where marked OCR. He gives battalions and squadrons, not men, for the corps on the march, and no strength for the troops in the position at Mariazell. His about 4000 is the corps after its retreat, including Khevenhüller's brigade, which joined it at Graz after the engagement (OCR) and was not at Mariazell. The passages read do not say whether Mariassy's 6 battalions and 6 squadrons are those left at Gross-Ramming. Bodart's 7,000 (claim bodart-strength) is in none of the passages read. The corps was present before the engagement, so the claim is tagged inherited. claims.value: Side B (Austrian), side A's report: Davout wrote to Berthier that the advanced guard had met, ahead of Neuhaus, the corps of General Merfeld (Merveldt), 6 battalions of grenadiers and 3 regiments of infantry strong, and that the colonels of the regiments Colloredo and Deutschmeister and 3 majors were among the prisoners.
claims.rationale: Side A's report of side B, read from the page image of Alombert and Colin's print of it, dated at Mariazell, 18 brumaire an XIV (9 November 1805). It gives units, not men, and names no source for them; Davout also sent a report made on the prisoners' declarations (claim side-a-information), which is not printed in the passages read. Alombert and Colin's narrative calls the corps the small corps of General Merveldt (claim bodart-winner) and gives no strength. Schönhals names the regiments Josef Colloredo and Deutschmeister among Merveldt's troops (claims schoenhals-side-b and side-b-command). The corps was present before the engagement, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'Davout to Berthier'; 'Mariazell, 18 brumaire year XIV'; 'I have the honour to report to Your Excellency that yesterday, toward 9 o'clock in the morning, the advanced guard, under the orders of General Heudelet, met ahead of Neuhaus the corps of General Merfeld, 6 battalions of grenadiers and 3 regiments of infantry strong'; 'the colonels of the regiments of Colloredo and Deutschmeister and 3 majors are among the prisoners'.

claims.value: Side A (French), the troops engaged: Davout reported that the advanced guard under General Heudelet met Merveldt's corps ahead of Neuhaus and attacked; Heudelet praised the 13th light infantry regiment and the 108th of the line, of which 5 companies led by Colonel Hygonnet charged the enemy as he tried to rally at Mariazell, and praised General Eppler and the adjudant-commandant Marès. In Alombert and Colin the 108e pursued for two hours and a squadron of the 7th hussars continued the pursuit on the road to Bruck; that night the rest of the cavalry bivouacked at Mariazell, the 13e léger at Siegmund and the 108e between that chapel and Wegscheid, while the corps' divisions bivouacked between Mariazell and Gaming along the road; in their narrative the carabiniers and voltigeurs of the 13e léger met a handful of Austrian grenadiers (OCR), and in the 3rd corps' journal the brigade of General Eppler met the enemy near Neuhaus (OCR). Schönhals writes that only a detachment of Davout's corps under General Heudelet followed Merveldt into the mountains, that Merveldt himself admitted the pursuing enemy never deployed more than 200 horse, and that Rittmeister Mengen reported a column of light infantry and some cavalry. In the list of the Grande Armée at 6 brumaire an XIV (28 October 1805 by our conversion) printed in t. IV, the 13e légère has 2 battalions among the troops of the 1st division of the 3rd corps (General Bisson, with Eppler among its generals of brigade) and the 108e de ligne 2 battalions among those of the 2nd division (General Friant, with Heudelet among its generals of brigade).
claims.rationale: No passage read gives side A's engaged strength in men, and Bodart's about 15,000 (claim bodart-strength) is not reconciled with the accounts, which have only the advanced guard engage. The list of 6 brumaire, the targeted follow-up, gives battalions, not men, eleven days (our arithmetic) before the engagement; by it the 13e léger and the 108e had 4 battalions together (our sum) on 28 October. The passages read do not give the advanced guard's composition beyond the regiments named. Schönhals does not say where Merveldt made his admission of 200 horse. The troops were with the advanced guard before the engagement, so the claim is tagged inherited. claims.value: Side A was Marshal Davout's corps, and the fighting was done by its advanced guard under General Heudelet. In Alombert and Colin (OCR), Davout's orders for the next day's march, given the day before, had the generals of division march their artillery even by night, and at Gaming he found that he could not reach Mariazell with his artillery and sent it back to the main road by Wieselburg. By Davout's report of the next day, the advanced guard met Merveldt's corps ahead of Neuhaus and Heudelet attacked with the greatest vigour without considering the enemy's numbers; 5 companies of the 108th under Colonel Hygonnet charged the enemy with the bayonet as he tried to rally at Mariazell; Davout then set Heudelet on the pursuit of the remains, which had withdrawn toward Lilienfeld. In Alombert and Colin's narrative (OCR), the carabiniers and voltigeurs of the 13e léger carried the first position near Neuhaus with a charge; at Mariazell the tirailleurs climbed the wooded mountain to the right of the road while a company on the left made for Mariazell to cut the retreat on Lilienfeld, and the 108e, held in reserve at Rasing, formed in column, crossed the bridge and advanced at the charge along the road, threatening to cut the enemy in two. The 108e pursued for two hours and near Wegscheid made 2,000 men lay down their arms, and a squadron of the 7th hussars continued the pursuit on the road to Bruck.
claims.rationale: Side A's decisions as the accounts give them (page images except where marked OCR). Heudelet commanded the troops engaged and decided to attack (Davout's report); Davout commanded the corps, ordered the march and the pursuit and dated his report at Mariazell the next day, but the passages read do not show him on the field during the fighting. Alombert and Colin's account of the fighting is read only in the OCR, and its figures are not restated. English renderings (ours): 'for the next day's march, Davout renews his recommendations:' (OCR); '"the generals of division will march their artillery, even by night, in order to gain as much ground as possible"' (OCR); 'having arrived at Gaming, Marshal Davout had recognized that it was impossible to reach Mariazell with his artillery, and had sent it back to the main road by Wieselburg' (OCR); Davout, as in claims davout-side-b and side-a-engaged for the meeting, the attack and the charge; 'I have set General Heudelet, to finish his work, in pursuit of these remains, which have withdrawn toward Lilienfeld'; Alombert and Colin, as in claim side-a-engaged for the carabiniers and voltigeurs; 'at last the charge is beaten and the position carried, after a short and bloody mêlée' (OCR); 'our tirailleurs, climbing the mountain to the right of the road through the woods, slowly drove back those of the enemy' (OCR); 'and made its way toward Mariazell to cut the retreat on Lilienfeld' (OCR); 'the 108th, held in reserve at Rasing, formed in column, crossed the bridge and advanced at the charge along the road' (OCR); 'the enemy, threatened with being cut in two by this attack, withdrew in all haste' (OCR); as in claim side-b-losses-reported for the 108e's pursuit and the hussars.

claims.value: FML (in Bodart GM) Count Merveldt commanded side B. In Schönhals, at Steyer, against all the representations of the quartermaster-general's staff, he resolved to unite with the Russians by St. Pölten and drew up the disposition by which the corps was to reach Annaberg in three strong marches by Reith, Neuhaus and Mariazell; the artillery reserve was sent ahead to Graz and the baggage toward Leoben. On the march he promised a reward for every gun brought to Neuhaus that day, ordered General Schustek, who now had to take over the rearguard, to push a grenadier battalion into the valley toward Gaming, and went ahead to Neuhaus with the head of the corps. On the 8th, when the French fell on the troops near Neuhaus and took the guns, Lieutenant-Colonel Volkmann and Rittmeister Mengen threw some hastily gathered grenadiers against them, and when Merveldt himself attacked with a body of troops he had gathered, the enemy was taken in the middle and one of his light battalions laid down its arms; but the disorder was too great for this to be exploited or the prisoners carried off. Merveldt then took a favourable position below Mariazell on the road to Bruck, occupied the height of Mariazell with infantry and placed a division of uhlans in the town. When the French seized houses in the valley below Zell, the grenadier battalion Riese defended them under Major Oscher; to secure the line of retreat, Schloss St. Sigmund was occupied by two companies of Josef Colloredo, and other detachments sent against the enemy's left flank made him fall back a little. Merveldt went off to Wegscheid, sending three squadrons of uhlans with some infantry ahead, and left General Mondet the order to withdraw from the position at nightfall. When the French attacked again on both wings, Mondet left the position somewhat earlier; the withdrawal was not made in proper order, the detachments covering the right flank left their posts, and the column, fired on from the height in the defile, broke up; the efforts of Mondet and the staff officers to restore order were in vain, and about 30 enemy horsemen cut into the last part of the column. In Alombert and Colin (OCR), Merveldt, giving up reaching Sankt Pölten, had chosen an excellent position on the road to Bruck.
claims.rationale: Side B's decisions as Schönhals gives them (page images except where marked OCR); Alombert and Colin's account of the march follows his closely (open question on families). Schönhals prints the position's distance below Mariazell as '12 Stunden', twelve hours, which does not fit the position at the height of Mariazell that he goes on to describe; the figure is not restated. Judgments, not recorded facts: Schönhals writes that Merveldt's reproaches to the troops were not unfounded but that it rested with him alone to spare the outposts' honour and himself this disgrace; that the panic was the more excusable because the troops were driven into a narrow valley whose sides were held by enemy tirailleurs; that the regiments Colloredo and Deutschmeister would have done the same as before if better led; that at the most decisive moment the general went off to Wegscheid, as he says in his report to the Hofkriegsrath, to look for a position, which did not need his presence; that he placed part of his cavalry at Mariazell, where it could do nothing, and sent the other half to Wegscheid, leaving the infantry in the defile without protection; that one squadron with the rearguard would have punished the 30 daredevils; that not one gun was left in the position to cover the retreat; and that at Neuhaus and Mariazell the troops were abandoned by their leader, who kept hurrying back to restore his favourite echelon order. English renderings (ours): 'against all the representations of the quartermaster-general's staff, Merveldt here formed the firm resolve to unite with the Russians by St. Pölten, and drew up the disposition by which the corps was to reach Annaberg in three strong marches by — Reith, Neuhaus and Mariazell —'; 'the artillery reserve was sent ahead to Graz, the baggage toward Leoben'; as in claim mariazell-ground for the reward for the guns; as in claim schoenhals-side-b for the battalions at Lunz, Schustek's rearguard and the head of the corps; 'Merveldt therefore ordered General Schustek to push a grenadier battalion forward into the valley leading toward Gaming, which was to hold there until the grenadiers of the rearguard had passed Lunz'; as in claim side-b-information for Mengen's report; 'when the French had advanced to almost half an hour from Neuhaus, Lieutenant-Colonel Volkmann of the quartermaster-general's staff and Rittmeister Wilhelm Mengen threw themselves against them with some grenadiers gathered in haste'; as in claim bodart-commanders for Merveldt's own attack; 'the disorder' (p. 128) 'of the surprised Austrian troops was, however, so great that neither could this advantage be used nor the prisoners already made be carried off' (p. 129); 'the corps commander therefore took a favourable position "12 Stunden" (as printed) below Mariazell on the road to Bruck'; 'the height of Mariazell was occupied with infantry, and a division of uhlans posted in the town itself'; 'hardly had the troops here gathered themselves somewhat when the enemy impetuously seized several of the houses lying in the valley below Zell, and so cut off the troops posted in front of Mariazell, of whom the division of uhlans went round the Schneeberg by the Lilienfeld road and rejoined the corps at Fürstenfeld'; 'the grenadier battalion Riese defended these houses with great bravery, in which the activity of its commander, Major Oscher, had great merit'; as in claim fortification-schoenhals for the castle; 'some other detachments, sent into the enemy's left flank, forced him to fall back a little'; they threatened the Austrians' right flank from Mariazell and climbed the heights to the left of the occupied castle'; 'this decided General Mondet to leave the position somewhat earlier'; 'the withdrawal was not made in proper order; the detachments posted' (p. 129) 'to cover the right flank left their posts on seeing the column march off, and they had hardly passed the occupied castle on the far side when the French, with loud shouts, attacked it and threw the two companies down and back through the water' (p. 130); 'from here the enemy, spreading out on the height, now fired on the column in the defile with such effect that it was thrown entirely into disorder, broke up into a shapeless lump, and, as the ground widened, everything burst out to left and right'; if it is true that 30 enemy horsemen sufficed to throw a column of six admittedly decimated battalions into disorder and take the greater part of it prisoner, it rested, however, with him alone to spare the honour of the Austrian outposts and himself this disgrace'; 'it is a known thing that in war the bravest troops are often seized by a sudden panic; it was here all the more excusable since they were driven into a narrow valley whose sides were held by enemy tirailleurs, who with every shot brought death and confusion into the troops'; 'the regiment Colloredo had fought very bravely at Steyer, and the regiment Deutschmeister had also behaved well in the position of Mariazell; these troops would without doubt have done the same if they had been better led'; 'but at the most decisive moment the general went off to Wegscheid, in order, as he says in his report to the Hofkriegsrath, to look for a position'; 'part of his cavalry he placed at Mariazell, where it could do nothing at all and was cut off at the first rush; the other half he sent to Wegscheid, and so left the infantry entangled in the defile without any protection'; 'a squadron with the rearguard would have punished the boldness of 30 daredevils'; as in claim means-and-supply for the guns; claims.value: Bodart records a victory of side A (French) under Marshal Davoust over side B (Austrian) under GM Count Meerveldt on 8 November. Davout reported that the Austrians were broken and put to the most complete rout, and that all that remained of the corps would have been taken had the steep, ice-covered roads allowed the cavalry to charge and reach the head of the column. In Alombert and Colin the victory almost entirely destroyed General Merveldt's small corps, whose remains could reach the Semmering. In Schönhals, things stood fairly well for the Austrians until sunset; after the renewed French attack the column broke up in the defile, the last part of it was taken, and only two grenadier battalions, 200 men together, could be formed as a rearguard before Wegscheid.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome (side A won), read from Bodart's entry, with the other accounts' ending, read from the page images. No source read gives a different result. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '1805 8/11. engagement at Mariazell (5.)'; as in claim bodart-strength for the entry; Davout, 'the Austrians were broken and put to the most complete rout: they left 400 dead on the field of battle, 600 wounded and 4,000 prisoners, 16 pieces of cannon and 3 flags'; 'all that remains of this corps would have been taken if the steep roads, all covered with ice, had allowed the cavalry to charge and reach the head of the column'; Alombert and Colin, 'this victory almost entirely destroyed the small corps of General Merveldt, who had withdrawn by Steyer and Weyer, and whose remains were able to reach the Semmering'; Schönhals, 'things stood fairly well on the Austrian side until sunset'; as in claims side-b-command and schoenhals-side-b for the fire into the column and the 30 horsemen.

Davout: 400 dead left on the field, 600 wounded and 4,000 prisoners, 16 guns and 3 flags; the colonels of the regiments Colloredo and Deutschmeister and 3 majors among the prisoners; 5 companies of the 108th took 1,500 prisoners in their charge; much baggage fell into French hands, but the vehicles were thrown into the ravines because they blocked the road; he sent the three captured flags with an aide-de-camp. claims.rationale: Separate accounts, read from the page images except where marked OCR, not combined. The counts differ: Davout and Bodart 4,000 prisoners and 16 guns, Alombert and Colin about 4,000 prisoners and 18 guns, and Schönhals a whole loss of 2500 men, which he gives in the passive ('wird ... angegeben', is given) without naming its source; Davout 3 flags, Alombert and Colin 2. Alombert and Colin's narrative and the 3rd corps' journal (OCR) give a number of guns taken near Neuhaus that is not restated; the journal says that everything that had fought on the plateau of Sigmund was taken and that the captured Austrian artillery went to Sankt Pölten (OCR). English renderings (ours): Davout, as in claim bodart-winner for the rout, as in claim davout-side-b for the colonels and as in claim side-a-engaged for the charge; 'I send Your Excellency, by one of my aides-de-camp, the three flags taken from the enemy'; 'much baggage fell into our power, but as the vehicles were blocking the road, we were forced to throw them into the ravines'; Alombert and Colin, 'but only a part could get ahead of our column. claims.value: Bodart places Mariazell, a market town in Styria on the Salza, 16 km north-east of Bruck an der Mur. In Schönhals, from Höllenstein on there was no road and the way was so bad that the last battalions reached Lunz only in the evening; behind Lunz a steep ridge separates the Lunz valley from the Langenau valley, hard to pass at any time and now, in the rainy season, glazed with ice, so that the guns could be moved over it only by men's hands; from the Langenau valley Neuhaus lay three hours away, with two steep hills still to climb, and the last defile lay between Langau and Neuhaus. Below Mariazell the line of retreat ran in a very narrow valley whose sides the French tirailleurs held, and Schloss St. Sigmund stands on a sheer rock wall close to the far bank of the Salza. Davout reported that the steep roads were all covered with ice, which kept his cavalry from charging, and that from Gaming to Mariazell there were very high, ice-covered mountains impossible to cross even by force of arms and horses. In Alombert and Colin the tirailleurs were delayed by the difficulties of the ground, and the hussars had great trouble crossing on the ice the col between Mariazell and Neuwiesen. In their narrative (OCR) the Austrians held the woods to the right of the road, the village of Rasing, the plateau of Saint-Sigmund and the amphitheatre of Mariazell, with the main body of their infantry deployed on the ridge that runs down between Mariazell and Rasing, facing north-west; the defile beyond Neuhaus was flanked by almost inaccessible mountains with tirailleurs on their tops; and, by the journal of Friant's division they quote, the valleys were extremely narrow. In the journal of Davout's corps (OCR) the enemy held the amphitheatre of Sigmund and the heights to right and left, his front covered by the little Salza, and the roads were covered with ice.

Side A: Davout reported that despite every human effort artillery and caissons could not follow, a great part having stayed between Waidhofen and Gaming; he took as many cartridges as possible with him and judged that in the mountains the enemy's artillery would be of no use to him either. In Alombert and Colin (OCR), Davout sent his artillery back from Gaming to the main road by Wieselburg; his order of the day before reminded the army that the moment had come to make forced marches and to suffer privations of bread; in the corps' journal the infantry was worn out and could march no further, having gone without stopping to eat, the divisions' artillery waited at Gaming for another route, and the captured Austrian artillery went to Sankt Pölten. In Schönhals the French had not yet had time to bring up artillery and could oppose none at all.

claims.value: Soon after the corps reached Reith in the night, news came that the enemy had already attacked the uhlans at Waidhofen, thrown them and was pursuing toward Gaming. On the 8th, as the detachments were arriving in the position near Neuhaus, Rittmeister Mengen galloped up to report that the enemy, having driven the uhlans from Gaming, had taken the road from Gaming toward Neuhaus with a column of light infantry and some cavalry and had fallen on the troops, who expected no attack and were busy moving their artillery over the mountain. open_questions: Deferred: Alombert and Colin's introduction after the selected passage for 7 November (p. 113, the 1st and 2nd corps), for 8 November at Saint-Pœlten (pp. 117-122) and after the selected passage (Beaumont's and Marmont's marches, pp. 125-126), and for 9 November (pp. 126-130), read and not cited; the 3rd corps' journals of 16 and 18 brumaire and the Journal de l'artillerie du 3e corps, seen only around keyword hits; the rest of the list of 6 brumaire for the 3rd corps (its 3rd division and its light cavalry division, p. 725), read only in the OCR and not cited; Davout's report on the prisoners' declarations and the detailed report of the combat he promised (p. 651), neither printed in the passages read; Merveldt's report to the Hofkriegsrath, which Schönhals cites, not inspected; Schönhals's account of the retreat after the engagement (p. 130, OCR), cited only for Graz, Khevenhüller's brigade and Fürstenfeld. Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: the hours of Merveldt's departure from Saint-Georgen, of the French advanced guard's start and of the infantry's day in the journal; the distances in Alombert and Colin's narrative; the number of guns taken near Neuhaus in their narrative and in the journal; the journal's count of the hussars' prisoners, which differs from the 150 printed on p. 125; the number of battalions of Khevenhüller's brigade; the page numbers of the parents, read from the OCR except where a page image is cited.

Most consequential gap: side A's engaged strength. Bodart gives about 15,000 men, but Davout's report and Schönhals have only Heudelet's advanced guard engage, and no passage read gives its strength. The targeted follow-up searched t. IV's appendix of situations for a return of the 3rd corps: there is none among the particular situations (pp. 748-770), and the list of the Grande Armée at 6 brumaire an XIV (28 October), read from the page images of pp. 711, 723 and 724, gives the 13e légère and the 108e 2 battalions each but no men (claim side-a-engaged). That narrows the gap to the composition of the advanced guard without closing it. A return of the 3rd corps for early November, Heudelet's detailed report of the combat or the 3rd corps' situations in the French war archives, none of which the passages read print, could close it.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side A's strength (Bodart about 15,000; the accounts have only Heudelet's advanced guard engage, with no figure, and Schönhals has Merveldt admit no more than 200 horse); side B's strength (Bodart 7,000; Davout 6 grenadier battalions and 3 infantry regiments; Schönhals 13 battalions and 6 squadrons leaving Steyer, with no count of men in the position); side B's loss (Bodart 4,000, mostly prisoners, and 16 guns; Davout 400 dead, 600 wounded and 4,000 prisoners, 16 guns and 3 flags; Alombert and Colin about 4,000 prisoners, 18 guns, 2 flags and 80 vehicles, and 150 more prisoners; Schönhals 2500 men in all, many of the scattered men soon returning); Merveldt's rank (Bodart GM, Schönhals FML); St. Sigmund (Schönhals a castle held by two companies, Alombert and Colin a chapel), and with it the fortification code (B_fortified from Schönhals, none_named from Alombert and Colin). Side A's loss is unknown in all three accounts.

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his 4,000 and 16 guns equal Davout's figures, though the passages read do not show his source); Alombert and Colin, t. IV (the French official history of 1908, with Davout's report of 9 November, the 3rd corps' journal and the list of 6 brumaire that it prints, all read as printed there, not as originals; its account of Merveldt's march to Neuhaus, and of the warning that reached him there, follows Schönhals's closely without citing him, and it cites Schönhals once elsewhere, so for Austrian-side statements it may not be independent of him; the passages read do not show whether the two share a source such as Merveldt's report); Schönhals (the Austrian account written in 1831 and printed in 1873, an interested one, which cites Merveldt's report to the Hofkriegsrath and gives French figures at second hand; by its preface, what it says of the French army's operations is drawn from that army's bulletins, which were not inspected).
